title: Cleaning and Decontamination

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Clean and decontaminate reusable instruments before sterilization, following manufacturer instructions and facility policy.
- Handle and transport contaminated instruments safely to prevent sharps injuries and cross-contamination.
- Select, don, use, and remove personal protective equipment correctly during instrument cleaning and decontamination.
- Recognize and escalate safety concerns, equipment problems, and exposures in instrument processing.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Decontamination is like rinsing the big mess off a plate before you wash it properly, so the plate is safe to pick up and the soap can reach the surface.

### Question 2

Germs can hide under dried-on dirt like a bug hiding under a rock. You have to wash the dirt away so the heat or germ-killing steam can reach every spot.

### Question 3

Bioburden is the amount of germs and grime sitting on a tool. The more there is, the harder it is to make the tool clean and safe.

### Question 4

If you spill spaghetti sauce, you wipe it up right away before it dries into a crust. Point-of-use cleaning is doing that quick wipe before the mess hardens.

### Question 5

It is much easier to wash a bowl that was left in water than one with dried-on oatmeal. Keeping tools moist works the same way.

### Question 6

Enzymatic detergent is like a special cleaner that 'eats' the dried bits of food and blood off a tool so they loosen up and wash away.

### Question 7

Cleaning sharp, dirty tools needs tough rubber gloves, like the thick ones you wear for scrubbing with harsh cleaners, not the thin ones you use once and throw away.

### Question 8

When you scrub dishes, water can splash up at your face. If those dishes had germs on them, you would want goggles to keep the splashes out of your eyes.

### Question 9

A waterproof apron is like the one you wear to protect your clothes when you paint or wash dishes, so messy splashes stay off your shirt.

### Question 10

Wash your hands before you put gloves on and again after you take them off, just like washing before and after a messy job.

### Question 11

Carrying dirty, sharp tools is like carrying a spillable drink; you use a closed, sturdy container with a lid so nothing leaks or pokes through.

### Question 12

Sharp tools are like loose thumbtacks; you keep them in their own spot and point them safely so nobody gets poked by surprise.

### Question 13

A used needle is like a tiny, germy spear. You drop it straight into the special hard box made for needles, without putting the cap back on.

### Question 14

You would not wash muddy boots next to clean folded laundry. Keeping the messy washing spot away from the clean storage spot stops the mess from spreading.

### Question 15

It is like a one-way street: clean things keep moving forward to the clean side and never turn back around into the muddy side.

### Question 16

After washing a dish, you check the cracks and hinges for stuck-on food before putting it away. Inspecting tools is the same careful look.

### Question 17

A toy with pieces that snap apart gets cleaner when you take it apart first, because the dirt hiding between the pieces gets washed away too.

### Question 18

If you wash a clothespin while it is clamped shut, the inside stays dirty. Open it up so the water can clean the part that pinches together.

### Question 19

After you soap up a glass, you rinse off the soap so you do not get a soapy drink. Instruments are rinsed so no cleaner is left behind on them.

### Question 20

You would not pack a wet towel into a sealed bag, because it could get mildewy. Tools are dried first so they do not trap dampness that lets germs grow.

### Question 21

Scratching a smooth pan with steel wool makes little grooves where food sticks. Scratched tools get little grooves where germs hide, so we clean them gently.

### Question 22

A glove with a hole is like a raincoat with a hole; you swap it for a dry, whole one before you keep working.

### Question 23

Soap cleans a plate, but putting it through the hot dishwasher is the step that kills the germs. Cleaning and germ-killing are two different jobs.

### Question 24

If you wash a bowl with dried egg using very hot water, the egg cooks and sticks harder. Using warm water keeps the egg from getting stuck so it washes off.

### Question 25

An ultrasonic cleaner shakes the water with invisible sound waves so hard that tiny bubbles pop and scrub the dirt out of the nooks and crannies of the tool.

### Question 26

You rinse the big chunks off a plate and make sure it is all the way under the water in the sink before the suds can work on it.

### Question 27

If you scrub a paintbrush under the water, the paint splatters less than if you scrub it in the air. Scrubbing tools under water keeps the germs from splashing around.

### Question 28

A drinking straw has an inside that gets dirty. You need a tiny brush to scrub the inside of the straw, and hollow tools need the same inside cleaning.

### Question 29

You would not stick your hand into murky water that might have broken glass in it. With sharp tools, you set them in carefully and never reach in where you cannot see.

### Question 30

Never poke your hand into water you cannot see through, because there might be something sharp hiding in there that can cut you.

### Question 31

A sharps box is a hard, sturdy box with a lid that used needles cannot poke through, so nobody gets stuck by accident.

### Question 32

You change a full trash bag before it overflows. A needle box is changed when it reaches the fill line, so no needles stick out the top.

### Question 33

You throw a used needle into the special box right where you are, right away, instead of carrying it around or leaving it for someone else.

### Question 34

To pick up something sharp, you use a grabber tool and keep the point away from people, like using tongs for hot food instead of your fingers.

### Question 35

If something gets in your eye, you rinse it with lots of water right away and tell an adult. The same rule applies at work, and the adult is your supervisor.

### Question 36

If you spill something messy on your arm, you wash it with soap and water right away and tell someone in charge, instead of just drying it off.

### Question 37

If you get cut by a dirty tool, you wash it and tell the person in charge right away, because they will help you get checked by a doctor or nurse.

### Question 38

You take off the dirtiest thing first, your gloves, then the rest, and wash your hands at the end, so the dirt never travels back onto your skin or face.

### Question 39

Get dressed from the inside out: put on the gown, then mask and goggles, and save the gloves for last so they cover your wrists.

### Question 40

You take off muddy boots before walking on clean floors. The same idea: remove dirty protective gear before you step into the clean part of the office.

### Question 41

Heavy rubber gloves are like your reusable kitchen gloves: you wash them, check for holes, and let them dry before using them again.

### Question 42

Rules that protect workers from germs in blood cover everyone whose job might touch blood or body fluids, including the person who cleans the tools.

### Question 43

Cleaning products are like a cake recipe: you have to use the right amounts and steps, or it will not work. More soap does not always mean cleaner.

### Question 44

Some cleaning liquids are like vinegar and baking soda, but much more dangerous: mixed together they can make harmful fumes, so you never mix them.

### Question 45

If you pour juice into a plain cup, you label it so nobody thinks it is water. Chemicals are labeled the same way, but it is even more important for safety.

### Question 46

When you clean with strong-smelling chemicals, you open a window so the fumes do not build up. The cleaning room needs good airflow for the same reason.

### Question 47

You would not wash your hands in the same bucket you used to scrub muddy tools. Separate sinks keep the clean-hands sink clean.

### Question 48

Dirty dishes go straight to the kitchen sink, not into the cupboard with the clean plates. Soiled tools go straight to the cleaning area.

### Question 49

To keep a dirty pan easy to wash later, you put some water in it so the food does not dry into a crust. Tools get a special moist spray for the same reason.

### Question 50

The container for dirty, sharp tools is like a sturdy, lidded bucket with a warning label, so nothing leaks out and nobody gets poked.

### Question 51

The grooved, grippy tips of tweezers catch little bits of stuff, so you scrub those ridges extra carefully, like brushing crumbs out of a textured surface.

### Question 52

If you rinse a glass with hard water, it can get cloudy spots. Tools are rinsed with good water so they do not get spots or buildup.

### Question 53

You would not use dish soap meant for plates to wash a delicate watch. Medical tools need the special cleaner made just for them.

### Question 54

You do not snack or put on lip gloss while your hands are covered in germy mess, because the germs could get into your mouth or onto your face.

### Question 55

Before using a reusable water bottle, you check it for cracks so it will not leak. Check rubber gloves for holes the same way.

### Question 56

Bath water gets dirty and stops being good for washing, so you drain it and start fresh. The ultrasonic cleaner's water is changed when it gets dirty too.

### Question 57

Some things only work at the right temperature, like yeast that needs warm water but not boiling water. Enzyme cleaners are the same.

### Question 58

Stain remover needs a few minutes to sit on a spot before it works. You have to wait the right amount of time for the cleaner to do its job.

### Question 59

The needle box sits right next to where the needles are used, standing up straight, so you can drop them in without walking around holding them.

### Question 60

You would not touch a clean white shirt with hands that just took out the trash. Clean up in between so the clean things stay clean.

### Question 61

Scrubbing messy, splashy dishes needs the full outfit: rubber gloves, a waterproof apron, and goggles so nothing splashes onto your skin or face.

### Question 62

A single-use item is like a paper cup: you use it once and throw it away, not wash it and use it again.

### Question 63

Dirty gloves and gowns go in the special marked trash can, not the normal one, so nobody else accidentally touches them.

### Question 64

You would not put a muddy boot on a clean kitchen counter. Dirty tools stay on the dirty side so they do not make the clean side dirty.

### Question 65

Your glove should go over your sleeve like a jacket over a shirt, so there is no gap where water could sneak in at your wrist.

### Question 66

If you spill something, you clean it up right away with the right supplies instead of leaving the mess for someone to step in.

### Question 67

It is like getting a dish ready to store: rinse the big mess, wash, rinse off the soap, dry, check it is clean, then put it away sealed and safe.

### Question 68

Hot water 'cooks' the blood onto the tool, like an egg cooking onto a pan, and once it is cooked on, it is much harder to scrub off.

### Question 69

If you stack plates in the sink, the ones underneath do not get soapy water on them. Spreading tools out in one layer lets the cleaning bubbles reach every one.

### Question 70

If something sharp falls into murky water, you fish it out with tongs or pour the water out carefully, so you never stick your hand where you cannot see.

### Question 71

If you spill a strong cleaner, you put on gloves and clean it up the safe way, because strong cleaners can hurt your skin.

### Question 72

If the washing machine stops washing, you do not keep using it and hope your clothes get clean. You stop, tell someone in charge, and get it fixed.

### Question 73

Think of three steps: first make it safe to touch, then wash off the dirt, then use the extra-hot cycle that kills every last germ.

### Question 74

Germs can hide under a blanket of dried blood, so the hot steam cannot reach them. You have to wash the blanket off first.

### Question 75

Dried-on oatmeal is way harder to scrub off than fresh oatmeal. Letting tools dry dirty makes them much harder to clean later.

### Question 76

You peel off the dirtiest layer first, the gloves, so your clean hands never touch the mess again while you take off the rest.

### Question 77

Hard water leaves white spots on glasses. Using soft, clean water for the last rinse keeps spots off the tools.

### Question 78

You put the dirty tools in a lidded container with a little moisture so they stay safe to carry and easy to wash when you get there.

### Question 79

Some cleaners mixed together make poisonous fumes, like a science experiment gone wrong. If you see it about to happen, say stop and tell a grown-up in charge.

### Question 80

Needles need a strong, lidded box that cannot be poked through or leak. A cardboard box with a trash bag is not strong enough for that job.

### Question 81

If the right safety gear is missing, you do not do the dangerous job anyway; you stop and tell someone so you can get the proper gloves first.

### Question 82

A cracked tool is like a cracked cup; you do not keep using it, because it could break and it cannot be cleaned properly in the crack.

### Question 83

Once a shirt is washed and folded, you would not toss it back into the muddy laundry pile. Clean things stay on the clean side.

### Question 84

Gloves are like oven mitts that protect only your hands. When you scrub, splashes can hit your face and clothes, so you need goggles, a mask, and an apron too.

### Question 85

A plate can look clean but still have invisible germs. You still check carefully, especially the grooves and hinges, before trusting it is ready.
